newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Ireland turns up heat on EU colleagues.
newsitem.headline: Ireland turns up heat on EU colleagues.

text.p: Ireland turned up the heat on its European Union partners on Tuesday, seeking to speed up the EU's languishing treaty negotiations by asking countries in what circumstances they would give up their voting veto.
At the end of a two-day negotiating session, the EU president said it had handed its partners a questionnaire asking them when they would be willing to move to majority voting.

It is one of the most controversial issues facing the bloc as it tries to make itself run more efficient in preparation for bringing in a dozen or more members from eastern Europe and the Mediterranean.
Britain has refused to countenance any move towards majority voting; others have strong objections in specific areas.
"Obviously we would like delegations to respond (to the questionnaire), say within the next week or so," Noel Dorr, Irish chairman of the IGC's main negotiating group, said.
Ireland is under pressure to speed up the IGC negotiations -- which began formally in March -- in order to have a draft treaty ready by for an EU summit in December.
A special EU summit, designed to give the IGC a push, is also to be held in Dublin on October 5.

But despite the widespread calls for the talks to be speeded up, officials and diplomats said a number of countries were reluctant to take a stand at what they see as an early stage in the negotiations.
"If the past two IGCs are anything to go by, there will be a mad rush at the end," said one diplomat.
France, Germany, the European Commission and a number of other EU players have been urging progress in the talks, but officials said differences in the bloc remained.
Dorr said the questionnaire reflected the divisions.
There was no consensus on when something should be taken by a majority decision, so negotiators needed to look at the issue on a case-by-case basis.
Similarly, he said, negotiators had failed to agree on when the directly-elected European Parliament should be given blocking power over EU decisions.
This had meant negotiators had to use a European Commission proposal as a basis for a case-by-case study of the issue.
"No clear approach emerged, so we focused on the Commission paper," Dorr said.
The negotiators were also divided on how many European commissioners there should be in an enlarged EU.

Dorr said that while some large countries believed that having one commissioner per country in a larger bloc was an invitation to inefficency, smaller countries believed that having a commissioner was a way of guaranteeing them a voice.
"The balance seems to be on the side of the smaller countries," Dorr said.
